720	The ideal is to educate, not just shout the truth
721	from the rooftops, the Rebbe said in a footnote. What
722	Rav Yosef says to the Tanna: my students are sitting here.
723	What do you mean? You have to come and say: there are
724	no humble ones left, no rabbis, no wise men, so what will they think?
725	How did he put it? They would say to Rava: "Do not leave a living creature
726	behind." If you are mediocre, what, my children will want
727	to be wicked? You can't. A rabbi cannot say
728	the truth about himself. He has to respect himself, because
729	there are children here, students here, youngsters here.
730	He has to think how things will be interpreted. That is already
731	an enormous educational point in its own right, unrelated
732	to the essence of humility. But we want to sum up the
733	questions we asked. First, what is humility? How can one
734	grow great and stay small? What did Moshe Rabbeinu tell himself?
735	How could he stand before Pharaoh and yet be silent before
736	his sister? That doesn't go together so well, does it? The Torah
737	says we believe it, and we see that even
738	HaShem is moved by it. That means it is an
739	unnatural phenomenon. There is some depth here. Second, how
740	does humility bring strength? We said Moshe was humble, not
741	lowly; Aharon was lowly. And third, how can it be
742	that the humble man is aware of his humility? So humility
743	must be something other than what we think. And we
744	want to develop a very special point: humility
745	stems precisely from knowing your strengths, not
746	from your weaknesses. And let's say it in one
747	incredibly powerful sentence. When a person succeeds a little,
748	he thinks it is his own. He imagines it is thanks to
749	his own talents. When a person succeeds enormously, he knows
750	that it is HaShem. When a person earns 10,000
751	shekels a month, he says: well, I did this, I got
752	where I got. But when a person outpaces all his friends
753	and sees them from above, what does he do?
754	He looks up at heaven. He says: it was not my talents that brought me here. I have the same
755	talents as my brother and my sister. How did I become
756	unique in his generation? Because the crown was placed on me.
757	Moshe's humility came from knowing that he was a figure
758	the likes of whom never was and never will be. And so he felt
759	like a man on whom a crown was placed. He felt like a
760	courier carrying diamonds. A courier carrying diamonds
761	is not boastful. They chose me. The mission was placed on me. All
762	I need is not to mess up. Moshe's humility
763	did not stem from weakness. It stemmed, on the contrary, from knowing
764	that HaShem chose him out of all the nations, out of all
765	other people. And so, on one hand, it gave him
766	great firmness. HaShem stands behind me.
767	This is not my strength. On the other hand, it gave him
768	tremendous modesty. He never felt
769	entitled to anything. I did not create myself,
770	I did not make myself. HaShem chose
771	me precisely because he knew how great he is. He
772	understood that such greatness can only come from above.
773	It has nothing to do with me. HaShem simply
774	chose me. So what was his prayer? That I not
775	mess up, that I not ruin it, that I fulfill, that I
776	truly carry out the mission I received. What is this
777	like? Here is a lovely mashal.
778	The first Rebbe of Ger, the Chiddushei HaRim, was a disciple of
779	the Rebbe of Kotzk. He took a small Chassidic group in a small town,
780	Gora Kalwaria in Poland, and turned it into
781	a huge Chassidic court spanning the world before the war, a mighty
782	Chassidic movement.
783	After he passed away, he was a truly giant man,
784	an immense Torah scholar of course and a great leader, but
785	materially he saw much hardship in life: out of
786	13 children, I think 12 died in his lifetime, and
787	he was left with a daughter named Esther and a grandson, Yehuda
788	Leib, the Sfat Emet. The boy was 19, a youth of 19,
789	and the Chassidim choose the Sfat Emet to replace his grandfather,
790	the Chiddushei HaRim of Ger. He sits down on the
791	great chair of the Ger leadership in Poland.
792	He had Chassidim who were four times his age,
793	who had still seen the Rebbe of Kotzk, who had still received
794	Chassidut from the great Rebbe of Kotzk. Once one of the Chassidim
795	came in to him and said: Listen, the Chassidim accepted
796	you, I accept you too, I have no complaints, but
797	do you feel comfortable? How can you sit there,
798	a 19-year-old boy, on this great chair and speak with
799	people who are four times greater than you, who heard
800	Chassidut still from the Rebbe of Kotzk and surely from the Chiddushei
801	HaRim? How do you feel comfortable speaking to them? What
802	makes you fit for this? The Chiddushei HaRim said, I will
803	tell you a mashal, sorry, the Sfat Emet said, I will tell
804	you a mashal. A group of mountain climbers climbs Everest.
805	Some fell at the beginning, some fell in the middle, some split off
806	midway. Two or three out of the whole large group
807	managed to reach the top.
808	They reach the peak, panting, satisfied,
809	feeling they have touched the sky, and they see a little child
810	sitting at the summit playing in the sand.
811	In one moment all their illusion shattered. Look, a little child
812	does it. They say to him, how did you get
813	here? He says, "I didn't get here. I was born
814	here. I was born on the mountain." He wanted to hint to them:
815	I did not climb by my own strength. From the start, Heaven
816	gave me, they chose me, they gave me the strength.
817	So these are not my strengths, they are HaShem's strengths.
818	But what is he teaching them? A wise person
819	is one who does not draw the source of his strength
820	from his own ego, he draws it from the One who chose him. A wise
821	person is one who lives constantly with the feeling:
822	HaShem expects something of me. If HaShem
823	expects something of me, on one hand he remains a mensch. It is not
824	his, he is not entitled to anything. HaShem
825	chose him, so he remains a mensch. On the other hand, it is the One
826	who gives him strength to succeed more and more. On the other
827	hand, he demands much more of himself.
828	I want to say an enormous point. I saw in the Ramban, I
829	don't remember if we once spoke about this in a class, maybe
830	yes, a few years ago.
831	It is the idea that a person should understand what his talent is, that a person
832	should understand what his talent obligates him to, that a person should understand
833	how much the talent is an obligation and not only a privilege. I once saw
834	an enormous point in the Ramban, about what is probably the strangest
835	story in the Torah. There is no doubt that if we look for
836	the story that seems the most out of place, unrelated,
837	it is the story of Bilam's donkey. What is this story?
